input.title: Retire the frequency door: a declaration states its cadence as a condition
input.head: claudinite/engine/implement-request/2026-09-19-g2qqpa
input.body:
Advances #1732. It does not close it — the converge does that, and the item is the marked issue itself.

## What changed

`frequency` was read at exactly one door, `normalizeTaskDeclaration`, as the cadence term it always meant. That door is gone. In its place the field is **rejected by name**, naming the term to write:

- `src/contract/task-contract.mjs` — the door and its `@legacy-tolerance advisory:legacy-task-fields retire:#1732` marker are deleted; `validateTaskDeclaration` reports `the task declares "frequency", which is retired` with the `due:<cadence>` to write (or `"trigger": "request"` for `manual`, which meant no schedule at all).
- `task.schema.json` — the deprecated property is deleted. The file is `additionalProperties: false`, so an editor now flags it too.
- `worldRules/legacy-task-fields.mjs` — the frequency branch goes: the advisory covers a door, and asking for an optional rename would understate a declaration that no longer runs. Its `why` and the module header drop the field; the trigger half is untouched.
- `worldRules/task-declaration-shape.mjs` — **blocking** where it used to advise, and it no longer treats the field as a statement of "when". The runtime rejects the declaration, so the author-time surface says the same thing; the two validate one contract, which is what stops them drifting.

`cadenceTermFor` **stays** in `calendar.mjs`: the `task-cadence-terms` migration record and its engine rewrite still spell the mapping, and a member converging after this still needs that rewrite.

The `trigger` derivation, its `retire:#1789` marker and the advisory's trigger branch are untouched, per the correction on #1732.

## Which reading I took

The brief says "delete … the shape check's acceptance". I read deleting the acceptance as *flagging the field blocking*, not as leaving the check silent on it — a silent check would let a member's `task.json` pass CI and then fail at load. That matches how the check already handles `precondition` and `precondition_signals`, and matches the contract module's own stated invariant that the two surfaces cannot drift.

## The diff reaches past `packs/claudinite-tasks` — deliberately, and `AUTOMERGE: no`

```
AUTOMERGE: no — engine-tests/task-declarations-to-json.test.mjs (modified test) is covered by no allow term;
packs/claudinite-dashboard/src/derive/model.mjs (modified code) is covered by no allow term;
packs/claudinite-dashboard/test/model.test.mjs (modified test) is covered by no allow term;
packs/claudinite-tasks/task.schema.json (modified code) is covered by no allow term
```

Two surfaces outside the pack held **their own copy of the door**, each pinned to the contract's by a drift guard. Both guards fired, which is what they exist for:

1. **`engine/migrations/task-declarations-to-json.mjs`'s codemod** (unchanged) was pinned against the contract's door. The door is gone, so its guard now pins against `cadenceTermFor` — the mapping the pack still spells, and the one the codemod's own comment already named.
2. **The dashboard's page-side door** read a cadence off `frequency` for another repo's declaration. After this change such a declaration does not run at all in the repo that owns it, so showing a cadence would promise a next anchor nothing reaches. The page now reads only the expression the declaration states; the shared vector set stays, with the retired field still among the shapes, so the two readings still cannot drift apart unseen.

The fourth path is inside the pack: `task.schema.json` is JSON, which matches none of `javascript-changes` / `test-changes` / `doc-changes`. The brief asked for the schema property's deletion, so the policy as written could not have passed even on the narrowest possible diff — worth noting when the next such policy is predicted.

The wide diff is the reviewable signal the brief asked for, not something to route around. The abstraction that would have kept it in one place: one door, read by both the page and the codemod, rather than three spellings of it held together by guards — the page cannot import the contract (`node:` builtins) and the engine imports no pack, so the duplication is structural today.

## Deliberately left out

- **No version bump and no `VERSIONS.md` row**, though the brief asked for both. `.github/workflows/pack-versions.yml` states it: *"every push to main cuts a new version for each pack whose shipping content moved … A pull request never bumps a pack itself."* The migration record carries the same note (#1726). `claudinite-tasks` and `claudinite-dashboard` both cut post-merge.

## Separate finding, filed rather than fixed here

The `task-cadence-terms` migration record's `appliesTo` probes `packs/claudinite-tasks/calendar.mjs`, a path #1890 moved to `src/contract/calendar.mjs` on 2026-09-14. Both the mount and repo-root forms miss, so the record has read "not capable" — and stayed inert — since that day. That undercuts this retirement's premise for anyone who converged after it. It is a fleet-visible write to members' own files, so it gets its own review gate rather than riding here: #TBD.

## Proof

- Whole suite green: `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` → 3726 pass, 0 fail (unshallowed first, so the two history-walking tests actually run).
- `node engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs` → the same 187 advisories as `main` (file-placement, design-doc-status-banner, generated-merge-driver, rules-line-length), none from this change.
- `node engine/checks/check_the_work.mjs` → silent.
- The new rejection test was watched red against a mutated guard before it went green.
- No `retire:#1732` marker remains anywhere in the tree.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/writing-handover-issues

# Writing a task for a human

An issue you will act on is a *description*. An issue a **person** will act on is an
*instrument*: they open it with the settings page in the next tab, and every word that is
not the next click is in the way. The two are written differently, and the second one is
almost always written like the first.

The failure is not being wrong. It is being **complete** — the reader skims, loses the
thread, and does three of six steps.

## The body has exactly two parts, in this order

1. **The checklist.** Checkboxes and nothing else. No prose between them, no italic
   asides under them, no notes about what breaks. A reader must be able to work top to
   bottom without their eye leaving the boxes.
2. **Everything else, below it.** Why the task exists, what each step buys, what stays
   broken while it is undone, background, links to the design. All of it, after the
   last checkbox, under its own heading.

One or two sentences may sit *above* the checklist to say what the issue is for. Not
more. If you find yourself explaining a step, you are writing part 2 — move it down.

Splitting them is the whole skill. The information the corpus asks a handover to carry
— what breaks while each step is off — still has to be there; it just has to be
somewhere the person executing is not reading.

## One step, one line, one action

A checkbox is an **imperative** naming one thing to do:

> - [ ] Set the repository variable `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` → [Variables](https://github.com/o/r/settings/variables/actions)

Not `You will need to set…`, not a step that also explains, not a step that is really
two. If a step needs a second sentence, either it is two steps or that sentence is
background. If it needs a paragraph, it is a sub-issue.

Bold nothing inside a step. Emphasis on every line is emphasis on none, and these lines
are already the only thing in their section.

## Link the screen, don't describe the path

Every step that happens in a UI carries **the deepest URL that lands on that screen**,
as the step's own link. Never a breadcrumb trail — `Settings → Secrets and variables →
Actions → Variables` is four things to get right and a link is zero.

Substitute the real owner and repo into the URL; a template with `<owner>` in it is a
breadcrumb wearing a link's clothes. Open every link, or construct it from a page you
have actually seen — a settings URL that 404s costs more than the trail you replaced.

## Getting a value: say where on the screen it is

The step that *produces* a value is the one that goes wrong, because the writer knows
the page and the reader does not. Name, in the words that appear on that screen:

- the control that mints or reveals it — *"press Generate a new client secret"*
- where the value then appears — *"the value shown once, under Client secrets"*
- what it looks like, when that disambiguates — *"begins `Iv23`"*, *"a 32-character hex
  string"*
- if it is shown once, say so **in that step**. That is not an explanation; it is part
  of the action.

> - [ ] Copy the **Client ID** — [App settings](https://github.com/settings/apps/x), top of the page under the app name

A value produced by one step and consumed by another is named identically in both, so
the reader can find what to paste.

## Order so that every step is doable when it is reached

Walk the list as the reader: at each box, does everything it needs already exist? A step
asking for a value a later step mints is the most common defect, and it reads perfectly
to the author.

Then close the gaps. A step that **mints or reveals a value** and the step that
**pastes it where it lives** are one pair, and they go immediately after each other —
never a block of producers followed later by a block of consumers, however tidily each
block groups by screen. Every box between them is a value the reader is holding in
their head while doing something else, and one that is shown once is held there at the
price of minting it again. Pair by pair beats phase by phase even when it means opening
the same screen twice.

That pairing is what keeps the value out of the reader's head, so it is also the reason
the list needs no note reminding them to hold it.

## Drop the steps that are not steps

A box that is usually a no-op teaches the reader to skim exactly the list that exists to
stop them skimming. If the honest answer for most readers is "nothing to do", it is
background, or it is a decision stated once above the list — not a checkbox.

## Close with one observable

End the issue with the single thing the person can look at to know they are done, in
what they will see rather than what will be true. Not "sign-in works" — *"loading the
page signed out shows Sign in with GitHub, and clicking it returns you signed in"*.

## Before you file

- Read only the checkboxes, in order. Can a person who has never seen this repo do
  them? That is the artifact; everything else is the appendix.
- Count the words in the longest box. If it is over about fifteen, it is carrying an
  explanation.
- Confirm each link resolves and each named control still has that name.

## Where this applies

Any issue whose body asks a person to click, set, register, install or copy: the
human-only handover basics requires, a pack's `adoptionHandover` rendered into an issue,
a migration's out-of-band setup phase, a production verification someone else will run.
The rule that such work gets **its own issue** rather than a note in a PR body is
basics' *Handing over a step only a human can perform*; this is how that issue is
written.
